title: When God Seems Like the Enemy
overview: A poet mourns the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, insisting the LORD himself has done this, and ends with the city crying out to God over its dying children.

parts.label: The Lord acts like an enemy (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: "Daughter Zion" pictures Jerusalem as a woman, the "footstool" most likely means the temple, and a "horn" stands for strength. The deepest shock is not the invading army but the sense that God himself has drawn his bow against his own people.

parts.label: Temple and worship wiped out (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Verse 6 is debated: God either tears down his temple like a flimsy garden shelter or rips away the protective hedge around his holy place, and either way the festivals and weekly day of rest can no longer be kept. The enemy's victory shouts inside the temple bitterly echo the joyful crowds who once sang there at festival time.

parts.label: Walls down, leaders gone (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: A measuring line, normally a builder's tool, here marks out what to demolish, showing the ruin was deliberate and thorough. With the king in exile and no teaching or prophetic word left, the elders sit silent in dust and rough sackcloth, the usual signs of deep mourning.

parts.label: Children starving in the streets (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: The poet says his insides are poured out on the ground (the Hebrew names the liver, which people then saw as the seat of feeling), meaning grief has emptied him completely. During the long siege, small children ask their mothers for food and die in their arms.

parts.label: No comfort, false prophets, mockery (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: The poet can find no other disaster to compare that might console, and he blames prophets who offered soothing lies instead of naming the people's wrongs. Passersby mock the city with its own proud titles, while the poet insists this is what God warned of long ago.

parts.label: Cry out and protest (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: The city is urged to weep through the night and plead for its children. Jerusalem then speaks to God directly about mothers eating their babies in the famine and priests killed in the temple, and the poem ends with that raw accusation and no answer.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the poem's picture of God as an enemy should be read mainly as a true account of deserved judgment, as verses 14 and 17 suggest, or mainly as an honest cry of anguish that Scripture preserves without endorsing every claim it makes.
think: What do you think is gained, or lost, when a poem about terrible suffering refuses to end with comfort?
